[^1683]: Typological interpretation of the bronze serpent set up upon a pole by Moses in the wilderness (Numbers 21:8–9), fulfilled in the lifting up of the Son of Man upon the Cross (John 3:14–15).

[^1684]: The martyrs exalted as sons and brethren of Christ and joint-heirs of His heavenly kingdom, having shared in His suffering and death (Romans 8:17; Hebrews 2:11–12).

[^1685]: Vivid hymnographic enumeration of the varied bodily torments endured by the early Christian martyrs (crucifixion, piercing with lances, sword-strokes, immersion in fire and water, wheel-breaking).

[^1686]: Traditional patristic and hymnographic metaphor of Christ as the mystical Cluster of Grapes (*Botrys*) suspended upon the Tree of the Cross, whose crushed juice yields the life-giving wine that dispels the intoxication of carnal passions.

[^1687]: The foundational Byzantine soteriological principle of *theosis* (deification): God became man from the Virgin's pure blood in order that man might be made partaker of the divine nature.

[^1688]: Typological parallel between the Babylonian furnace, which did not burn the Three Youths, and the virginal womb of Mary, which was unconsumed by the divine fire of the Godhead.

[^1689]: Ode 8 heirmos of the Canon of the Cross, Tone 2, based on the Song of the Three Holy Children (Daniel 3:57).

[^1690]: Typological reflection upon the life-giving stream of blood and water flowing from the side of the crucified Savior (John 19:34), drying up the rivers of pagan polytheism and watering the Church with true piety.

[^1691]: The cosmic convulsions accompanying the Crucifixion of Christ recorded in Matthew 27:45, 51–52: the solar eclipse, the rending of the temple veil, the splitting of rocks, and the harrowing of hell.

[^1692]: Allusion to Psalm 67:36 [LXX 67:36 / MT 68:35]: "Marvelous is God in His saints," affirming the miraculous curative power resident in the relics of the holy martyrs.

[^1693]: Acclamation of the heroic endurance of the passion-bearers amidst wild beasts, foul stables, extreme cold, scorching heat, and torture.

[^1694]: Allusion to Galatians 3:13: "Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us."

[^1695]: Ode 8 heirmos of the second canon, praising the Lord who preserved the Hebrew youths in the furnace.

[^1696]: Marian invocation uniting the title of the Theotokos as the immaculate Ewe-lamb (*Amnas*) with Christ as the Lamb of God (*Amnos tou Theou*, John 1:29).

[^1697]: Allusion to 1 Thessalonians 5:5: "Ye are all the children of light, and the children of the day."

[^1698]: Allusion to Christ as the fountain of Living Water (John 4:10; 7:37–38) brought forth through the virginal conception.

[^1699]: Ode 9 heirmos of the Canon of the Cross, Tone 2, drawing upon Luke 1:78–79 (the Dayspring from on high visiting those in darkness) and John 11:52 (gathering together into one the scattered children of God).

[^1700]: Allusion to the suffering servant prophecy of Isaiah 53:5: "He was wounded for our transgressions... and with His stripes we are healed."

[^1701]: Ancient Christian tradition based on Isaiah 60:13 concerning the three species of wood comprising the Holy Cross: cypress, pine, and cedar, symbolizing the incorruptibility, fragrance, and majesty of Christ's sacrifice, combined with the Chalcedonian confession of one hypostasis in two natures.

[^1702]: Patristic imagery of Satan vanquished and made a laughingstock like a captured sparrow, drawn from Job 40:24 [LXX] / 41:5: "Wilt thou play with him as with a bird?"

[^1703]: Affirmation of the double destiny of the martyrs: their earthly blood hallows the soil, while their sanctified spirits join the angelic hierarchies before the divine throne.

[^1704]: Stavrotheotokion of Ode 9, lamenting the paradox of the Creator of all nature hanging upon the wood of the Cross.

[^1705]: Ode 9 heirmos of the second canon (to the Theotokos), Tone 2, celebrating the renewal of fallen Adam through the Incarnation of God the Word.

[^1706]: Classical Byzantine catalog of Marian epithets: steadfast protectress (*prostates*), expectation (*elpis*), wall (*teichos*), firm shelter (*skepē*), and unshakable harbor (*limēn*).

[^1707]: Church Slavonic `чꙋжда́гѡ` corresponds to the Greek `τοῦ ἀλλοτρίου` ("the stranger" / "the alien"), referring to the devil and demonic thoughts invading the human soul.

[^1708]: Allusion to Hebrews 2:14, affirming that through His death on the Cross Christ destroyed him that had the power of death, that is, the devil.

[^1709]: Psalm 89:14, 16 [LXX 89:14, 16 / MT 90:14, 16], serving as the first Psalm stichos for the daily Matins aposticha.

[^1710]: Allusion to 2 Corinthians 8:9: "For ye know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that, though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor, that ye through His poverty might be rich."

[^1711]: Psalm 89:17 [LXX 89:17 / MT 90:17], serving as the second Psalm stichos for the daily Matins aposticha.

[^1712]: Martyrikon sticheron extolling the universal honor accorded to martyrs' relics, citing their lawful struggle (2 Timothy 2:5).

[^1713]: Concluding lines of the Tone 2 Stavrotheotokion prosomoion to the model "When from the Tree" (*Egda ot dreva*), continued from physical leaf p205.

[^1714]: Opening troparion of the Beatitudes at Divine Liturgy on Wednesday, recalling the penitent thief upon the cross (Luke 23:42).

[^1715]: Allusion to John 12:32: "And I, if I be lifted up from the earth, will draw all men unto Myself."

[^1716]: Theological reflection on Colossians 2:14: "Blotting out the handwriting of ordinances that was against us, which was contrary to us, and took it out of the way, nailing it to His cross."

[^1717]: The martyrs glorified as partakers of the sufferings and subsequent eternal glory of Christ (Romans 8:17; 1 Peter 4:13).

[^1718]: Trinitarian doxological troparion of the Beatitudes, confessing the consubstantiality and co-eternity of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

[^1719]: Stavrotheotokion concluding the Beatitudes on Wednesday.

[^1720]: Canonical H2 day opening for Thursday in the Octoechos cycle, commemorating the Twelve Holy Apostles and Saint Nicholas, Archbishop of Myra in Lycia.

[^1721]: Typological allegory identifying the Apostles with the four mystical rivers of Eden (Genesis 2:10), whose preaching irrigated the whole earth and harvested souls for the kingdom of God.

[^1722]: The Apostles characterized as radiant rays and eyewitnesses (*autoptai*, Luke 1:2) of Christ, the true Sun of Righteousness and Dayspring from on high (Luke 1:78; Malachi 4:2).

[^1723]: Apostolic typology contrasting the stone tablets of the Mosaic Law with the living tablets of the new covenant in the Holy Spirit (2 Corinthians 3:3; Luke 11:20).

[^1724]: Celebrated hymnographic wordplay between the city of Myra in Lycia (where Saint Nicholas presided as archbishop) and the sweet-smelling spiritual myrrh (*myron*) of his virtues and post-mortem wonderworking relics.

[^1725]: Supplication unto Saint Nicholas as the swift deliverer of those tempest-tossed upon the sea of life and beset by sudden tribulations.

[^1726]: Applying the Dominical title "light of the world" (Matthew 5:14) to Saint Nicholas, whose radiant life illumines souls darkened by sinful passions.

[^1727]: Apostolic Theotokion synthesizing the Incarnation of the Word with the worldwide missionary commissioning of the Apostles.

[^1728]: Allusion to Acts 5:15, recording that the inhabitants of Jerusalem brought forth the sick into the streets, that at least the shadow of Peter passing by might overshadow them.

[^1729]: Psalm 122:1–2 [LXX 122:1–2 / MT 123:1–2], the first Psalm verse appointed for the daily Vespers aposticha.

[^1730]: Allusion to the cry of the terrified disciples during the tempest on the Sea of Galilee (Matthew 8:25): "Lord, save us: we perish!"

[^1731]: Psalm 122:3–4 [LXX 122:3–4 / MT 123:3–4], the second Psalm verse appointed for the daily Vespers aposticha.

[^1732]: Martyrikon apostichon praising the holy martyrs as heavenly physicians capable of healing bodily and spiritual afflictions after their earthly departure.

[^1733]: Metaphor of the Mother of God as the fruitful olive tree in the house of God (Psalm 51:10 [LXX 51:10 / MT 52:8]).

[^1734]: Ode 1 heirmos of the Supplicatory Canon to the Theotokos at Small Compline on Wednesday evening, based on the Exodus canticle of Moses (Exodus 15:1–2).

[^1735]: Canonical hymnographic refrain addressed directly to the Mother of God throughout the Compline canon.

[^1736]: Ode 3 heirmos of the Compline canon, invoking the tree of the Cross which abolished sin.

[^1737]: Church Slavonic `благопремѣ́нна` translates the Greek liturgical term `εὐδιάллаκτον` ("easily appeased," "reconciled," "propitiated"), entreating the Theotokos to make God merciful to penitent sinners.

[^1738]: Christ addressed as the Hypostatic Wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1:24) carried in the arms of the Theotokos.

[^1739]: Ode 4 heirmos of the Compline canon, derived from the canticle of the Prophet Habakkuk (Habakkuk 3:2).

[^1740]: Ode 5 heirmos of the Compline canon, based on Isaiah 26:9.

[^1741]: Allusion to Romans 10:4: "For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to every one that believs."

[^1742]: Conclusion of the supplication of Ode 5, continued from physical leaf p209.

[^1743]: Penitential Ode 6 heirmos of the Compline canon, based on Psalm 129:1 [LXX 129:1 / MT 130:1].

[^1744]: Allusion to Isaiah 61:10 and the spiritual robe of righteousness defiled by sin and restored to joy.

[^1745]: Allusion to Ephesians 1:7 and Revelation 1:5: Christ who washed us from our sins in His own blood.

[^1746]: Sessional Hymn (Sessional Hymn) of the Compline canon, set to the melodic model "We have become partakers of the divine" (Greek: Θείας γεγόναμεν / Church Slavonic: Бж҃твеннагѡ бы́хомъ), an incipit drawn from 2 Peter 1:4 ("that by these ye might be partakers of the divine nature").

[^1747]: Ode 7 heirmos of the Compline canon, commemorating the Three Youths who refused to bow down to the golden idol erected by Nebuchadnezzar on the plain of Dura (Daniel 3:1–18).

[^1748]: Allusion to Colossians 2:14 on Christ tearing asunder the handwritten record of our debt upon the Cross.

[^1749]: Allusion to the lamentation of Psalm 68:21 [LXX 68:21 / MT 69:20]: "I looked for some to take pity, but there was none; and for comforters, but I found none."

[^1750]: Patristic imagery of the white baptismal robe (*chiton*) tarnished through negligent sin and washed clean through repentance and Marian intercession.

[^1751]: Opening words of the Ode 8 heirmos of the Compline canon, catching at the bottom of physical leaf p210 and continued on physical leaf p211.

[^1752]: Ode 8 heirmos conclusion of the Supplicatory Canon to the Theotokos at Small Compline, Tone 2, drawing upon the Song of the Three Holy Children in the Babylonian furnace (Daniel 3:57).

[^1753]: Troparion of Ode 8, pleading for freedom from passions (*apatheia*) and divine illumination amidst the assault of vices.

[^1754]: Troparion of Ode 8, praising the Mother of God as a tower of strength (allusion to Proverbs 18:10), ladder/step (*bathron* / *stepen'*), and steadfast protectress of the faithful.

[^1755]: Doxasticon of Ode 8, confessing the Word of the immortal Father born of the Virgin Mary, delivering from death all who praise Him.

[^1756]: Theotokion of Ode 8, invoking the Virgin Mary as the ungrudging fountain of healings for believers.

[^1757]: Ode 9 heirmos of the Compline canon, derived from Luke 1:78–79 and celebrating the Incarnation of God the Word to renew fallen Adam.

[^1758]: Troparion of Ode 9, addressing the Theotokos as the Mother of the true Life (John 14:6) and conduit of eternal celestial food.

[^1759]: Troparion of Ode 9, invoking the Virgin as the Gate of divine light (*porta lucis*), dispelling demonic gloom by her immaterial radiance.

[^1760]: Doxasticon of Ode 9, entreating the Mother of God to heal spiritual and physical sicknesses and loosen the bonds of sorrow.

[^1761]: Concluding Theotokion of the Compline canon, confessing the Chalcedonian dogma of the pre-eternal Son born of the Father becoming perfect man in the womb of the Virgin.

[^1762]: Rubrical directive concluding Small Compline with the Marian megalynarion *Axion Estin* ("It is truly meet"), the Trisagion prayers, Our Father, troparia, and the standard daily dismissal.

[^1763]: Opening of Thursday Matins in the weekly Octoechos cycle, dedicated to the memory of the Twelve Holy Apostles and Saint Nicholas, Archbishop of Myra in Lycia.

[^1764]: First Apostolic Sessional Hymn after the first stichology of the Psalter, celebrating Christ who made unlearned fishermen wiser than worldly rhetors (1 Corinthians 1:26–29) and sent them forth to preach the Gospel.

[^1765]: Psalm 18:5 [LXX 18:5 / MT 19:4], the standard apostolic verse applied by Saint Paul to the worldwide dissemination of the Gospel (Romans 10:18).

[^1766]: Second Apostolic Sessional Hymn after the first stichology, commemorating the disciples whose simple proclamation of the Cross confounded worldly philosophy.

[^1767]: Theotokion after the first stichology, addressing the Virgin Mary as the cloud of the unsetting Light (allusion to Isaiah 19:1).

[^1768]: First Apostolic Sessional Hymn after the second stichology, depicting the Apostles as fishers of men (Matthew 4:19) who drew all nations into the net of the Holy Spirit.

[^1769]: Psalm 88:6 [LXX 88:6 / MT 89:5]: "The heavens shall confess Thy wonders, O Lord," appointed as the first psalm verse of the second stichology.

[^1770]: Psalm 67:36 [LXX 67:36 / MT 68:35]: "Marvelous is God in His saints, the God of Israel," introducing the Martyrikon troparion.

[^1771]: Martyrikon troparion after the second stichology, praising the martyrs whose blood sanctified the earth and whose relics sanctify churches.

[^1772]: Theotokion after the second stichology, confessing the deification (*theosis*) of human nature made partakers of the divine nature (2 Peter 1:4) through Christ's Incarnation.

[^1773]: Melodic model (*Podoben*) heading: "Being the wellspring of loving-kindness" (*Miloserdïia sushchi istochnik* / Greek: Εὐσπλαγχνίας ὑπάρχουσα πηγή), an automelon of Tone 2.

[^1774]: Third Kathisma Sessional Hymn to the Apostles, invoking the Disciples as radiant luminaries enlightening the world under the sun (Philippians 2:15).

[^1775]: Sessional Hymn to Saint Nicholas, celebrating his miracles that dispel the gloom of tribulations.

[^1776]: Theotokion after the third stichology, imploring the Mother of God together with the Apostles to obtain forgiveness of sins and amendment of life.

[^1777]: The first Canon of Thursday Matins, composed by Saint Theophanes the Branded (Graptos, c. 778–845), dedicated to the Holy Apostles.

[^1778]: Ode 1 heirmos of the Apostolic Canon, drawing upon the Song of the Sea (Exodus 15:1–2) and the overthrow of Pharaoh's army in the Red Sea.

[^1779]: Troparion of Ode 1, portraying the Apostles as divine lightning-flashes (*fulgura divina*) dispelling the darkness of sensual pleasures.

[^1780]: Troparion of Ode 1, invoking the Apostles as friends of Christ (John 15:14–15) to rescue the soul that has befriended the devil through sinful deeds.

[^1781]: Troparion of Ode 1, comparing the deadened soul to Lazarus who lay four days in the tomb (John 11:38–44), praying for resurrection through apostolic prayers.

[^1782]: Theotokion of Ode 1, invoking the Virgin Mary who gave birth to the Good God, together with the Prophets, Martyrs, and Apostles.

[^1783]: The second Canon of Thursday Matins, composed by Saint Joseph the Hymnographer (c. 816–886), bearing an acrostic in the original Greek: "Accept a loving prayer, O Nicholas" (*Mōlbū liubēznū Nīkōlaē prīīmī* / Greek: Δεχου ποθητην, Νικολαε, προσφοραν).

[^1784]: Ode 1 heirmos of the Canon to Saint Nicholas, based on Exodus 15. The 1895 Lviv print exhibits an epigraphic haplography (*razdiel'shemu liudi* instead of *razdiel'shemu morie, i nastavľshemu liudi*), here faithfully translated as inked and noted.

[^1785]: Troparion of Ode 1 (St. Nicholas), describing the hierarch standing before the heavenly throne of grace (Hebrews 4:16) to obtain mercy for his flock.

[^1786]: Troparion of Ode 1 (St. Nicholas), exalting the saint as an earthly protector guarding believers day and night against demonic temptations.

[^1787]: Troparion of Ode 1 (St. Nicholas), employing the metaphor of Saint Nicholas as the daystar / morning star (*phosphoros*, 2 Peter 1:19), whose radiant beams dispel sinful darkness.

[^1788]: Theotokion of Ode 1 (Canon 2), supplicating the Mother of God to heal bodily sicknesses and spiritual wounds, delivering the soul from eternal fire.

[^1789]: Ode 3 heirmos of the Apostolic Canon, based on 1 Kingdoms 2:1–2 [1 Samuel 2:1–2] and Isaiah 35:1 ("the desert shall blossom as the lily").

[^1790]: Troparion of Ode 3, commemorating the unlettered Apostles who, instructed by the Father's Wisdom in the Holy Spirit, confounded Greek philosophy (1 Corinthians 1:20–21).

[^1791]: Troparion of Ode 3, praying that the spiritual barrenness of the soul may be transformed into the fruitfulness of virtuous deeds.

[^1792]: Troparion of Ode 3, beseeching Christ the Benefactor to heal the venomous bite of the serpent through the prayers of the Apostles.

[^1793]: Theotokion of Ode 3 (Apostles), entreating the Virgin Mary together with all the Apostles for deliverance from harm, adversity, and perils.

[^1794]: Ode 3 heirmos of the Canon to Saint Nicholas, celebrating Christ who mortified sin upon the Tree of the Cross and established believers in His fear.

[^1795]: Troparion of Ode 3 (St. Nicholas), addressing Christ as the divine Fountain of healings, preserving His servant unharmed.

[^1796]: Troparion of Ode 3 (St. Nicholas), entreating Saint Nicholas to restore the defeated mind and protect it against visible and invisible adversaries.

[^1797]: Opening of Troparion 3 of Ode 3 (St. Nicholas), confessing Christ the sole Good One who bestowed Saint Nicholas as a benevolent protector of mankind, continued on leaf p215.

[^1798]: Conclusion of Troparion 3 of Ode 3 (St. Nicholas), continued from leaf p214.

[^1799]: Theotokion of Ode 3 (Canon 2), praising the All-Spotless Virgin as strength, joy, gladness, and a firm wall of defense.

[^1800]: Ode 4 heirmos of the Apostolic Canon, derived from the Canticle of Habakkuk (Habakkuk 3:2–3): the Incarnate Lord coming not as an ambassador or an angel, but Himself in the flesh to save mankind.

[^1801]: Troparion of Ode 4, crying out for the spiritual food of salvation to nourish the soul starving amidst passions.

[^1802]: Troparion of Ode 4, typological imagery based on Habakkuk 3:8, 15: the Apostles as the horses of the Lord riding upon the sea of the world, troubling the bitter salt waters of unbelief.

[^1803]: Troparion of Ode 4, praising the Apostles who heralded Christ the Sun of Righteousness unto those in darkness, entreating them to enlighten the sinner and restrain evil thoughts.

[^1804]: Theotokion of Ode 4 (Apostles), asking the All-Hymned Mother of God to join the Apostles in intercession for deliverance from sins and afflictions.

[^1805]: Ode 4 heirmos of the Canon to Saint Nicholas, also drawing upon Habakkuk 3:2: hearing the Lord's report and being struck with awe at His condescension (*synkatabasis*) to seek the lost sheep.

[^1806]: Troparion of Ode 4 (St. Nicholas), venerating Saint Nicholas for adorning the episcopal throne of Myra with virtues, entreated to adorn the uncomely soul.

[^1807]: Troparion of Ode 4 (St. Nicholas), entreating the saint to smooth the path to heaven, calming worldly billows and guiding the soul to the harbor of eternal life.

[^1808]: Troparion of Ode 4 (St. Nicholas), invoking the hierarch as a hearer of divine words to deliver the supplicant from demonic snares and lawless men.

[^1809]: Opening of Theotokion of Ode 4 (Canon 2), supplicating the Mother of God for protection day and night against demonic assaults, continued on leaf p216.

[^1810]: Ode 5 heirmos of the Apostolic Canon, invoking 1 Timothy 2:5 ("one Mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus") and the transition from the night of ignorance to the light of the Father.

[^1811]: Troparion of Ode 5, depicting the Great Shepherd (Hebrews 13:20) sending His disciples as sheep amidst wolves (Matthew 10:16), transforming them by the power of holy baptism.

[^1812]: Troparion of Ode 5, the Apostles celebrated for enlightening hearts in the darkness of delusion with the divine light of the Gospel.

[^1813]: Troparion of Ode 5, penitential plea to Christ before the end, crying out for pardon for the sake of His Apostles.

[^1814]: Theotokion of Ode 5 (Apostles), the Theotokos addressed as the dwelling-place of Light, invoked alongside the Apostles for deliverance from distress.

[^1815]: Ode 5 heirmos of the Canon to Saint Nicholas, based on Isaiah 26:9: seeking God early and walking in the light of His commandments.

[^1816]: Troparion of Ode 5 (St. Nicholas), Saint Nicholas venerated as a faithful fulfiller of the Divine Law, asked to help believers keep the commandments and escape demonic harm.

[^1817]: Troparion of Ode 5 (St. Nicholas), alluding to the celebrated miracle of Saint Nicholas appearing in dreams to the Emperor Constantine and the prefect Ablabius to deliver three innocent Roman military officers (*stratēgai*) condemned to death.

[^1818]: Troparion of Ode 5 (St. Nicholas), Saint Nicholas invoked as Christ's sacred minister and guarantor/surety (*engyetēs*) for sinners before the judgment seat of God.

[^1819]: Theotokion of Ode 5 (Canon 2), the Virgin Mary addressed as the Mother of the Lord (*Kyriotokos* / *Gospodoroditelnitsa*), delivering the soul from violent passions.

[^1820]: Ode 6 heirmos of the Apostolic Canon, invoking the prayer of Jonah 2:2–3 from the belly of the whale and Psalm 129:1.

[^1821]: Troparion of Ode 6, the Apostles depicted as bearers of the Living Water (John 4:10, 7:38) to quench the soul parched by the scorching heat of sin.

[^1822]: Troparion of Ode 6 (Apostles), the Apostles celebrated as noetic heavens declaring the ineffable glory of God (Psalm 18:2 [LXX 18:2 / MT 19:1]).

[^1823]: Troparion of Ode 6 (Apostles), the sinner tempest-tossed upon the surging deep of life fleeing unto Christ the divine Helmsman (*Kybernētēs*).

[^1824]: Theotokion of Ode 6 (Apostles), the Bride of God entreating her Son in company with the heavenly angelic powers, Prophets, Apostles, and Martyrs.

[^1825]: Ode 6 of the Canon to Saint Nicholas uses the same heirmos ("Wallowing in the abyss of sin").

[^1826]: Troparion of Ode 6 (St. Nicholas), playing upon the name of Myra (*Myra* / *myron*), Saint Nicholas as primate perfuming the assembly of believers with sweet virtues and dispelling the stench of sin.

[^1827]: Troparion of Ode 6 (St. Nicholas), the heart of Saint Nicholas praised as shining brighter than the sun, dispersing the gloom of trials.

[^1828]: Troparion of Ode 6 (St. Nicholas), Saint Nicholas possessing the broad expanse of mercy, strengthening the sinner to tread the narrow way (Matthew 7:14) unto the Lord.

[^1829]: Theotokion of Ode 6 (Canon 2), constant recourse unto the Mother of God as a swift helper rescuing from grievous torment.

[^1830]: Ode 7 heirmos of the Apostolic Canon, commemorating the Three Youths in the furnace of Babylon, upon whom Christ spread a spiritual dew against the tyrant's decree.

[^1831]: Troparion of Ode 7, the Apostles ignited with the fire of the Holy Spirit at Pentecost (Acts 2:3–4), extinguishing the coals of demonic deception.

[^1832]: Troparion of Ode 7, the Apostles renouncing the world and worldly lusts (1 John 2:15–17) out of love for Christ who united Himself to mortal flesh.

[^1833]: Troparion of Ode 7, penitential supplication unto Christ the righteous Judge and Knower of hearts (Acts 1:24) not to condemn the sinner into eternal fire.

[^1834]: Opening of Theotokion of Ode 7 (Apostles), the Virgin Mary unconsumed by the divine fire of the Godhead, continued on leaf p218.

[^1835]: Conclusion of Theotokion of Ode 7 (Apostles), continued from leaf p217.

[^1836]: Ode 7 heirmos of the Canon to Saint Nicholas, celebrating the Three Hebrew Children refusing to worship the golden image on the plain of Dura (Daniel 3).

[^1837]: Troparion of Ode 7 (St. Nicholas), flying like a bird amidst the snares of daily temptation (Psalm 123:7 [LXX 123:7 / MT 124:7]), fleeing beneath the saint's protection.

[^1838]: Troparion of Ode 7 (St. Nicholas), urgent supplication to Saint Nicholas for swift aid amidst bodily distress and demonic afflictions.

[^1839]: Troparion of Ode 7 (St. Nicholas), recalling Saint Nicholas appearing in a dream unto the Emperor to rescue innocent men appointed to die.

[^1840]: Theotokion of Ode 7 (Canon 2), inscribing the Pure Virgin as the sole guardian of one's whole life and intercessor for the world.

[^1841]: Ode 8 heirmos of the Apostolic Canon, the fiery furnace in Babylon separating its operation, burning the Chaldeans while bedewing the faithful Hebrew youths (Daniel 3).

[^1842]: Troparion of Ode 8, the Holy Spirit descending upon the Apostles bodily in the likeness of fire (Acts 2:3), appointing them luminaries consuming godlessness.

[^1843]: Troparion of Ode 8, healing the unrectified heart tempest-tossed by passions, through the supplications of Christ's disciples.

[^1844]: Troparion of Ode 8, exhortation to the soul to weep bitterly before the arrival of uncomforted lamentation in the day of judgment.

[^1845]: Theotokion of Ode 8 (Apostles), the unburning furnace of Babylon prefiguring the virginal conception and childbearing of the Mother of God without corruption.

[^1846]: Ode 8 heirmos of the Canon to Saint Nicholas, the Song of the Three Holy Youths in the furnace (Daniel 3:57).

[^1847]: Troparion of Ode 8 (St. Nicholas), Saint Nicholas receiving from God the power to bind and loose (Matthew 16:19; 18:18), loosing the bonds of sins.

[^1848]: Troparion of Ode 8 (St. Nicholas), the divine visitation of Saint Nicholas smoothing the path of the humble soul day and night.

[^1849]: Troparion of Ode 8 (St. Nicholas), praying for Saint Nicholas to extend his helping hand and preserve the supplicant from bitter death, even as he once saved the condemned youths.

[^1850]: Troparion of Ode 8 (St. Nicholas), anticipation of the Dread Judgment Seat of Christ, asking not to enter into judgment with His servant (Psalm 142:2 [LXX 142:2 / MT 143:2]).

[^1851]: Theotokion of Ode 8 (Canon 2), the Virgin Mother of God exalting fallen mankind through her supernatural childbearing.

[^1852]: Ode 9 heirmos of the Apostolic Canon, the Son of the Unoriginate Father, God and Lord, incarnate of the Virgin to enlighten those in darkness and gather the scattered (John 11:52).

[^1853]: Troparion of Ode 9, the condemned and negligent soul entreating Christ to turn him back from demonic delusions through apostolic prayers.

[^1854]: Troparion of Ode 9, the glorious and all-wise Apostles invoked to deliver the faithful from all harm, wrath, sin, and distress.

[^1855]: Troparion of Ode 9, confession of an uncorrected soul and a conscience buried beneath mountains of transgression, continued on leaf p220.

[^1856]: Conclusion of Troparion 3 of Ode 9 (Apostles), continued from leaf p219.

[^1857]: Theotokion of Ode 9 (Apostles), the Apostles preaching Christ throughout the world as true God and true man, joined in prayer with the Mother of God at the Last Judgment.

[^1858]: Ode 9 heirmos of the Canon to Saint Nicholas, derived from Luke 1:78 and the Incarnation of God the Word to renew Adam fallen into corruption.

[^1859]: Troparion of Ode 9 (St. Nicholas), borrowing the famous incipit of the Troparion of Saint Nicholas: "A rule of faith and a model of meekness" (*Kanon pisteos kai eikon praotetos* / *Pravilo viery i obraz krotosti*).

[^1860]: Troparion of Ode 9 (St. Nicholas), Saint Nicholas as a sacred vessel of divine myrrh poured forth upon the earth, dispelling the foul odor of passions.

[^1861]: Troparion of Ode 9 (St. Nicholas), comforting the soul assailed invisibly by temptations stirred up day and night by the deceiver.

[^1862]: Troparion of Ode 9 (St. Nicholas), warning that the Dread Day of the Master is at the doors (Matthew 24:33), urging repentance before the end.

[^1863]: Theotokion of Ode 9 (Canon 2), pleading for the Lord's mercy at the Judgment, joined by the Virgin Mary, the apostolic choir, and Saint Nicholas.

[^1864]: Rubrical direction for the conclusion of Matins: *Axion Estin* with a prostration, Little Litany, Exapostilarion, and the usual Psalms of Praise.

[^1865]: Opening of the Matins Aposticha for Thursday, Tone 2, dedicated to the Holy Apostles.

[^1866]: First Apostolic Apostichon, celebrating the exalted names of the supreme Apostles whose mere shadows healed diseases (Acts 5:15), continued on physical leaf p221.

[^1867]: Conclusion of the first Apostolic Apostichon from leaf p220, praising the unlettered fishermen who, though simple Jews, theologized the sublime mysteries of divine grace.

[^1868]: Psalm 89:14, 16 [LXX 89:14, 16 / MT 90:14, 16], appointed as the first psalm verse of the Aposticha at Thursday Matins.

[^1869]: Second Apostolic Apostichon, incorporating the desperate cry of the disciples in the tempest-tossed boat on the Sea of Galilee: "Lord, save us: we perish" (Matthew 8:25).

[^1870]: Psalm 89:17 [LXX 89:17 / MT 90:17], appointed as the second psalm verse of the Aposticha at Thursday Matins.

[^1871]: Martyrikon troparion concluding the Thursday Matins Aposticha.

[^1872]: The ancient Marian prayer *All my hope do I place upon thee* (*Vse upovanïye moye na tya vozlagayu*), chanted at the close of the Matins Aposticha.

[^1873]: Liturgical rubric for the conclusion of Thursday Matins: Psalm 91:2 ("It is good to give praise unto the Lord"), Trisagion prayers, Our Father, daily dismissory troparia, and the Litany of Fervent Supplication.

[^1874]: First Beatitude troparion of Thursday Liturgy, invoking the Good Thief's cry from the cross (Luke 23:42). The printed text contains an epigraphic diminutive form or typographical error: *razboynichk'* (разбо́йничкь) for *razboynich'* (разбо́йничь).

[^1875]: Second Beatitude troparion, celebrating the universal mission of the Apostles delivering mankind from demonic darkness.

[^1876]: Third Beatitude troparion, employing the evangelical metaphor of the Apostles as fishers of men (Matthew 4:19) drawing souls from the sea of worldly vanity.

[^1877]: Fourth Beatitude troparion, commemorating the holy martyrs who finished the course and kept the faith (2 Timothy 4:7).

[^1878]: Doxasticon / Triadikon of the Beatitudes, confessing the uncreated Trinity and the co-equal divine operation (*homoenergeia*) of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

[^1879]: Concluding Marian Beatitude troparion, praising the Mother of God as the boast of the Apostles and crown of the martyrs.

[^1880]: Liturgical opening of the Friday cycle in Tone 2, dedicated to the Precious and Life-Giving Cross and the Passion of Christ, beginning on Thursday evening at Vespers.

[^1881]: First Sticheron of the Cross at Thursday Vespers, commemorating the cosmic upheavals attending the Crucifixion of Christ (Matthew 27:51–52; Luke 23:44–45).

[^1882]: Second Sticheron of the Cross, celebrating the overthrow of Satan and the liberation of Adam from the ancestral curse through Christ's elevation upon the Cross.

[^1883]: Third Sticheron of the Cross, depicting the harrowing of hades and the jubilation of the forefather Adam at Christ's voluntary passion.

[^1884]: Rubrical directive for the remaining Stichera on "Lord, I have cried": appointed from the Menaion, or alternatively from the supplementary Stavrotheotokia in Tone 2.

[^1885]: First Stavrotheotokion, the maternal lamentation of the Mother of God standing before the Cross of her Son.

[^1886]: Second Stavrotheotokion, recounting the piercing of Christ's side with a lance (John 19:34) and the anguish of the Theotokos.

[^1887]: Third Stavrotheotokion, depicting the Pieta / Deposition from the Cross, the Virgin embracing and kissing the dead body of Christ before burial.

[^1888]: Doxasticon Stavrotheotokion at the Stichera on "Lord, I have cried," portraying the Mother of God as the spotless Ewe-lamb beholding the Lamb of God led to slaughter (Isaiah 53:7).

[^1889]: Rubric for the standard evening order: the vesperal hymn *Phos Hilaron*, the Thursday evening daily prokeimenon ("My help comes from the Lord," Psalm 120:2), and the evening prayer *Kataxioson* ("Vouchsafe, O Lord").

[^1890]: First Apostichon of the Cross at Thursday Vespers, linking the saving power of the Cross with Christ stretching forth His hand to save the sinking Peter on the sea (Matthew 14:30–31).

[^1891]: Psalm 122:1, 2b [LXX 122:1, 2 / MT 123:1, 2], the standard first verse of the daily Vespers Aposticha.

[^1892]: Second Apostichon of the Cross, contrasting Christ's divine gifts with the crowd's demand for Barabbas and the condemnation of Jesus (Matthew 27:20–23).

[^1893]: Psalm 122:3a, 4 [LXX 122:3, 4 / MT 123:3, 4], the standard second verse of the daily Vespers Aposticha.

[^1894]: Martyrikon troparion concluding the Vespers Aposticha in Tone 2.

[^1895]: Doxasticon Stavrotheotokion at the Aposticha, meditating on the cosmic paradox of Christ hanging between thieves, He who suspended the earth upon the waters (Job 26:7).

[^1896]: Concluding rubrics for Thursday Vespers: the Canticle of Simeon (Luke 2:29–32), Trisagion prayers, Our Father, the Troparion of the Cross ("Save, O Lord, Thy people"), and the standard dismissal.

[^1897]: Ode 1 heirmos of the Supplicatory Canon to the Theotokos at Small Compline, Tone 2, drawing upon the Song of the Sea (Exodus 15:1).

[^1898]: Opening of Troparion 1 of Ode 1 (Compline Canon), praising the unmatched beauty and purity of the Virgin (Song of Songs 4:7), continued on leaf p224.

[^1899]: Conclusion of Troparion 1 of Ode 1, continued from leaf p223.

[^1900]: Troparion of Ode 1, quoting Psalm 44:10 [LXX 44:10 / MT 45:9]: "At Thy right hand stood the queen in a vesture of gold," praying for a place at Christ's right hand at the Last Judgment.

[^1901]: Doxasticon troparion of Ode 1, applying the metaphor of the parched furrow made fruitful by the Heavenly Rain of Christ's grace.

[^1902]: Concluding Marian troparion of Ode 1, contrasting the tree of the knowledge of good and evil (Genesis 2:17) with the Tree of Life, Christ incarnate of the Virgin.

[^1903]: Ode 3 heirmos of the Compline canon, drawn from Isaiah 35:1 and 1 Kingdoms 2:1 [1 Samuel 2:1].

[^1904]: First troparion of Ode 3, commemorating the Incarnation wherein the Creator assumes human nature to clothe Adam, stripped by sin, in the robe of incorruption (Genesis 3:21; Galatians 3:27).

[^1905]: Second troparion of Ode 3, beseeching God the Word to show mercy upon the soul grieving over sinful passions.

[^1906]: Doxasticon troparion of Ode 3, imploring the Theotokos to administer divine medicine against the venom of the ancestral serpent.

[^1907]: Concluding Marian troparion of Ode 3, pleading for maternal intercession to defend the faithful and overthrow the arrogance of the impious.

[^1908]: Ode 4 heirmos of the Compline canon, drawn from the Canticle of Habakkuk (Habakkuk 3:2–3) and Isaiah 63:9.

[^1909]: First troparion of Ode 4, praying for tears of compunction (*katanyxis*) to extinguish the burning inflammation of passions.

[^1910]: Opening of Troparion 2 of Ode 4, confessing the wounds inflicted by sinful pleasures, continued on leaf p225.

[^1911]: Conclusion of Troparion 2 of Ode 4, continued from leaf p224, appealing to the healing flow from the pierced side of the Crucified Lord (John 19:34).

[^1912]: Doxasticon troparion of Ode 4, supplicating the Mother of God, who possesses the riches of grace, to enrich the spiritually destitute soul.

[^1913]: Concluding Marian troparion of Ode 4, identifying Christ as the Father's Radiance (Hebrews 1:3) dispelling demonic darkness through His Crucifixion.

[^1914]: Ode 5 heirmos of the Compline canon, drawn from 1 Timothy 2:5 and Isaiah 26:9.

[^1915]: First troparion of Ode 5, confessing Christ as the Way (John 14:6) and pleading for deliverance from the precipice of sin.

[^1916]: Second troparion of Ode 5, alluding to the Parable of the Prodigal Son wasting his substance in a far country (Luke 15:13).

[^1917]: Doxasticon troparion of Ode 5, invoking the Virgin as a channel of living waters (John 7:38) quenching the flames of passions.

[^1918]: Concluding Marian troparion of Ode 5, citing the messianic prophecy of Isaiah (Isaiah 7:14). The 1895 Lviv print exhibits a typographical error: *i mela yesi* (и҆ мѣ́ла є҆сѝ) for *imela yesi* (имѣ́ла є҆сѝ).

[^1919]: Ode 6 heirmos of the Compline canon, drawn from the Canticle of Jonah (Jonah 2:3, 7) and Psalm 129:1 [LXX 129:1 / MT 130:1].

[^1920]: First troparion of Ode 6, begging that the soul be not surrendered to the mocking joy of demons at the Last Judgment.

[^1921]: Second troparion of Ode 6, presenting the Mother of God as an all-efficacious intercessor to appease the divine wrath provoked by sinful thoughts.

[^1922]: Doxasticon troparion of Ode 6, addressing the Theotokos as the Mother of the Supreme Judge.

[^1923]: Concluding Marian troparion of Ode 6, beseeching the Virgin Mother to intercede with Jesus the Savior for deliverance from tribulations.

[^1924]: Rubric directing the threefold *Kyrie Eleison*, *Doxa Patri*, and the chanting of the Sessional Hymn after Ode 6.

[^1925]: Stavrotheotokion Sessional Hymn following Ode 6 at Compline, contemplating the Mother of God's sorrow before the mystery of the voluntary Crucifixion.

[^1926]: Ode 7 heirmos of the Compline canon, based on the furnace of Babylon (Daniel 3:19–28).

[^1927]: First troparion of Ode 7, drawing upon Psalm 117:14 [LXX 117:14 / MT 118:14] ("The Lord is my strength and my song, and He is become my salvation").

[^1928]: Second troparion of Ode 7, confessing the deification (*theosis*) of human nature through the Incarnation of God from the virginal blood of Mary.

[^1929]: Doxasticon troparion of Ode 7, interpreting the unburning furnace of Babylon as a type of Mary's womb bearing the consuming fire of the Godhead unburnt.

[^1930]: Concluding Marian troparion of Ode 7, confessing the perpetual virginity of the Theotokos (*aeiparthenia*) before, during, and after childbearing.

[^1931]: Ode 8 heirmos of the Compline canon, based on Daniel 3:57.

[^1932]: First troparion of Ode 8, exhorting the soul to virtues under the patronage of the Mother of God.

[^1933]: Opening of Troparion 2 of Ode 8, invoking Mary's childbearing which dissolved the curse of Adam, continued on leaf p227.

[^1934]: Conclusion of Troparion 2 of Ode 8, continued from leaf p226.

[^1935]: Doxasticon troparion of Ode 8, addressing the Theotokos as Mother of the Radiance of the Father (Hebrews 1:3).

[^1936]: Concluding Marian troparion of Ode 8, praising Christ as the Sun of Righteousness (Malachi 4:2 [LXX 3:20]).

[^1937]: Ode 9 heirmos of the Compline canon, drawn from Luke 1:78–79 and John 11:52.

[^1938]: First troparion of Ode 9, contrasting the bitter taste from the tree of knowledge with the sweetness of immortality flowing from the Tree of the Cross.

[^1939]: Second troparion of Ode 9, addressing Mary as Queen and Mother of the King Who destroyed the realm of death.

[^1940]: Doxasticon troparion of Ode 9, pleading for entrance through the gates of repentance.

[^1941]: Concluding troparion of Ode 9, meditating on Christ's death upon the Cross putting the ancient serpent to death and reviving the deadened soul.

[^1942]: Rubrical conclusion of Small Compline: the Marian megalynarion *Axion Estin*, Trisagion prayers, Our Father, and dismissal troparia.

[^1943]: Opening of Friday Matins in Tone 2, dedicated to the Precious and Life-Giving Cross and the Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ.

[^1944]: First Sessional Hymn of the Cross after the first stichology of the Psalter, quoting Psalm 73:12 [LXX 73:12 / MT 74:12].

[^1945]: Psalm 98:5 [LXX 98:5 / MT 99:5], the standard psalm verse of the Holy Cross.

[^1946]: Opening of Sessional Hymn 2 after the first stichology, contrasting Adam's capture through the tree of Eden with Christ's captivity of Satan through the Tree of the Cross, continued on leaf p228.

[^1947]: Conclusion of Sessional Hymn 2, continued from leaf p227, invoking Christ as the Second Adam (1 Corinthians 15:45–47) seeking the lost sheep (Luke 19:10).

[^1948]: Stavrotheotokion after the first stichology at Friday Matins.

[^1949]: First Sessional Hymn after the second stichology. The rubric contains the official 19th-century Austro-Hungarian imperial prayer petition: *spasi imperatora (imkya)* ("save the Emperor [Name]"), referring to Emperor Franz Joseph I (reigned 1848–1916).

[^1950]: Psalm 73:12 [LXX 73:12 / MT 74:12], the second appointed psalm verse for the Cross at Friday Matins.

[^1951]: Second Sessional Hymn after the second stichology, the classic Troparion of the Holy Icon of Christ (*Prechistomu obrazu tvoyemu poklanyayemsya*), appointed here as a troparion of the Cross.

[^1952]: Psalm 67:36 [LXX 67:36 / MT 68:35], introducing the Martyrikon.

[^1953]: Martyrikon troparion after the second stichology, alluding to Psalm 146:8 [LXX 146:8 / MT 147:8] ("Who covers the heaven with clouds").

[^1954]: Stavrotheotokion concluding the second stichology at Friday Matins.

[^1955]: First Sessional Hymn after the third stichology, echoing Luke 23:42.

[^1956]: Second Sessional Hymn after the third stichology, invoking Christ as the Good Shepherd (John 10:11) seeking the hundredth lost sheep (Matthew 18:12–13; Luke 15:4–6).

[^1957]: Stavrotheotokion concluding the third stichology at Friday Matins.

[^1958]: The first Canon of Friday Matins in Tone 2, dedicated to the Precious and Life-Giving Cross, composed by Saint Joseph the Hymnographer (c. 816–886), bearing in Greek the alphabetical/thematic acrostic: *Staurou pagentos phrouda daimonon plana* ("When the Cross was planted, demonic delusion fell").

[^1959]: Ode 1 heirmos of the Canon of the Cross, derived from the Song of the Sea (Exodus 15:1).

[^1960]: First troparion of Ode 1 (Canon of the Cross), contemplating Christ accepting shameful crucifixion to confer eternal honor on humanity.

[^1961]: Second troparion of Ode 1, contrasting the stretching of the heavens like a curtain (Psalm 103:2 [LXX 103:2 / MT 104:2]) with Christ stretching out His hands upon the Cross to gather the nations.

[^1962]: Martyrikon troparion of Ode 1, praising the martyrs who took up their cross to follow the crucified Christ (Matthew 16:24; Philippians 3:10).

[^1963]: Second Martyrikon troparion of Ode 1, contrasting the rejoicing of angels with the lamentation of demons at the triumph of the martyrs.

[^1964]: Concluding Stavrotheotokion of Ode 1, citing the prophecy of Righteous Simeon: "Yea, a sword shall pierce through thine own soul also" (Luke 2:35).

[^1965]: The second Canon of Friday Matins in Tone 2, dedicated to the Most Holy Theotokos.

[^1966]: Ode 1 heirmos of the Marian Canon, based on Exodus 14–15.

[^1967]: First troparion of Ode 1 (Marian Canon), addressing the Virgin as Mother of the Fountain of dispassion (*apatheia*).

[^1968]: Second troparion of Ode 1, praying for healing of both somatic infirmities and spiritual passions.

[^1969]: Opening of Troparion 3 of Ode 1, appealing to the protection of the Mother of God, continued on leaf p230.

[^1970]: Conclusion of Troparion 3 of Ode 1 (Marian Canon), continued from leaf p229.

[^1971]: Fourth troparion of Ode 1, invoking the Mother of God as the true propitiatory / mercy-seat (*hilasterion* / *ochistilishche*, Exodus 25:17–22; Hebrews 9:5).

[^1972]: Ode 3 heirmos of the Canon of the Cross, drawn from the Canticle of Anna (1 Kingdoms 2:1–2 [1 Samuel 2:1–2]).

[^1973]: First troparion of Ode 3 (Canon of the Cross), employing the mystical typology of the cluster of grapes from the Promised Land (Numbers 13:23), Christ hanging upon the vine-tree of the Cross.

[^1974]: Second troparion of Ode 3, commemorating the voluntary elevation of Christ upon the Cross casting down Satanic tyranny.

[^1975]: First Martyrikon troparion of Ode 3, praising the martyrs whose spiritual fire quenched physical fire (Hebrews 11:34).

[^1976]: Second Martyrikon troparion of Ode 3, depicting the martyrs clothed in the purple of their own shed blood and wielding the Cross as a royal scepter (Revelation 7:14; 2 Timothy 2:12).

[^1977]: Concluding Stavrotheotokion of Ode 3, praising the Virgin whose Son loosed the bonds of death through the Wood of the Cross.

[^1978]: First troparion of Ode 3 (Marian Canon), entreating the Unoriginate King incarnate of the Virgin to preserve the believer from eternal condemnation.

[^1979]: Second troparion of Ode 3, beseeching the Virgin who bare the Ever-Living Fountain to grant tears of compunction.

[^1980]: Opening of Troparion 3 of Ode 3, praying for the healing of a soul wounded by demonic assaults and despondency (*akedia*), continued on physical leaf p231.

[^1981]: Conclusion of Troparion 3 of Ode 3 (Marian Canon), continued from physical leaf p230, entreating tears of repentance and holy fear.

[^1982]: Fourth troparion of Ode 3 (Marian Canon), lamenting a life spent in spiritual slothfulness (*akedia*) and seeking the Lady's compassion.

[^1983]: Heirmos of Ode 4, referencing the Christological citation of Isaiah 63:9 (LXX: "neither an ambassador, nor an angel, but He Himself saved them"). Note "therefore" used in place of pseudo-archaic "therefore".

[^1984]: First troparion of Ode 4, drawing an antithetical parallel between Christ's suspension on the Cross and His suspension of the earth upon the waters (Job 26:7), and the outflowing of blood and water (John 19:34).

[^1985]: Second troparion of Ode 4, presenting the Passion of Christ as the restorative reversal of the Fall of Adam and Eve.

[^1986]: First Martyrikon troparion of Ode 4, invoking the martyrs as physicians who draw healing grace from the springs of the Savior (Isaiah 12:3).

[^1987]: Second Martyrikon troparion of Ode 4, recounting the tortures of the martyrs—crucifixion, scourging, and flaying—as a total defeat of the demonic enemy.

[^1988]: Stavrotheotokion of Ode 4, depicting the weeping of the Theotokos as she contemplates the injustice of Christ's execution and His boundless loving-kindness.

[^1989]: Heirmos of Ode 4 (Marian Canon), paraphrasing Habakkuk 3:2 regarding the fearful report of God's coming in condescension to seek the lost.

[^1990]: First troparion of Ode 4 (Marian Canon), honoring the Mother of God as the rod that sprouted the transcendent Word.

[^1991]: Second troparion of Ode 4 (Marian Canon), pleading for the dews of the Virgin's grace to dissolve the fetters of sin.

[^1992]: Opening of Troparion 3 of Ode 4 (Marian Canon), continued on physical leaf p232, confessing passion-defilement before the spotless habitation of God.

[^1993]: Conclusion of Troparion 3 of Ode 4 (Marian Canon), continued from physical leaf p231.

[^1994]: Fourth troparion of Ode 4 (Marian Canon), employing nautical imagery of calm waters and the divine haven (*limen*).

[^1995]: Heirmos of Ode 5, uniting the live coal of Isaiah's vision (Isaiah 6:6) with the Sun of Righteousness emerging from the Virgin's womb.

[^1996]: First troparion of Ode 5, commemorating Christ's willing condescension to dishonor in order to seat restored humanity at the right hand of the Father (Ephesians 2:6).

[^1997]: Second troparion of Ode 5, contrasting the crown of thorns inflicted upon the Word with His crowning of creation with blossoms (Psalm 103:14 [LXX]).

[^1998]: First Martyrikon troparion of Ode 5, recalling 2 Corinthians 12:9-10 ("for when I am weak, then am I strong").

[^1999]: Second Martyrikon troparion of Ode 5, venerating the martyrs as heavenly advocates against earthly tribulations.

[^2000]: Stavrotheotokion of Ode 5, highlighting the divine paradox of the Cherubim-borne Word resting upon the arms of the Virgin and dying upon the Cross.

[^2001]: Heirmos of Ode 5 (Marian Canon), echoing Isaiah 26:9 ("From night early do I seek Thee, O God").

[^2002]: First troparion of Ode 5 (Marian Canon), addressing the Mother of the hypostatic Life (John 14:6) to revive a soul deadened by demonic traps.

[^2003]: Second troparion of Ode 5 (Marian Canon), beseeching the Mother of the Chief Shepherd to place the penitent among the sheep at the Last Judgment (Matthew 25:33).

[^2004]: Third troparion of Ode 5 (Marian Canon), pleading for liberation from demonic temptations ("the stranger") and gehenna.

[^2005]: Fourth troparion of Ode 5 (Marian Canon), supplicating the Bride of God to disperse the darkness of passions with beams of true repentance.

[^2006]: Heirmos of Ode 6, confessing Christ as the sole Author and Cause (*aitios*) of human salvation.

[^2007]: First troparion of Ode 6, applying Isaiah 50:6 ("I gave My back to the smiters, and My cheeks to them that plucked off the hair; I hid not My face from shame and spitting") to Christ's saving Passion.

[^2008]: Second troparion of Ode 6, referencing the Paschal lamb led to slaughter (Isaiah 53:7) who revives those fatally poisoned by the spiritual wolf (Satan).

[^2009]: First Martyrikon troparion of Ode 6, praising the martyrs who rejected the counsel of the ungodly (Psalm 1:1) to gain eternal life.

[^2010]: Second Martyrikon troparion of Ode 6, alluding to spiritual warfare against the principalities and powers (Ephesians 6:12).

[^2011]: Stavrotheotokion of Ode 6, stating the classic patristic theosis soteriology: God became man and suffered crucifixion in order to deify mankind and slay the ancient slayer.

[^2012]: Heirmos of Ode 6 (Marian Canon), echoing Jonah 2:2-6 ("Deep calls unto deep; out of the belly of Hades cried I").

[^2013]: First troparion of Ode 6 (Marian Canon), confessing the maternal boldness (*parrhesia*) and efficacy of the Virgin's intercession before her omnipotent Son.

[^2014]: Second troparion of Ode 6 (Marian Canon), crying for deliverance from the surge of grief and spiritual billows.

[^2015]: Third troparion of Ode 6 (Marian Canon), contrasting human cruelty with the compassionate mercy of the Mother of God.

[^2016]: Fourth troparion of Ode 6 (Marian Canon), citing the Johannine title of Christ (John 1:29: "Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world").

[^2017]: Heirmos of Ode 7, referencing the Three Holy Youths in the fiery Babylonian furnace (Daniel 3) and the spiritual dew bestowed by the pre-incarnate Christ.

[^2018]: First troparion of Ode 7, extolling Christ's lifting up upon the Cross as the cosmic co-elevation (*syn-egersis*) of fallen humanity and the nullification of Satan.

[^2019]: Second troparion of Ode 7, referencing Colossians 2:14 (nailing the handwriting of ordinances to the Cross) and the mocking reed (Matthew 27:29) transformed into the pen of manumission.

[^2020]: First Martyrikon troparion of Ode 7, describing how the bodily dismemberment of the martyrs was met with unbroken spiritual union with God and victory over the adversary.

[^2021]: Second Martyrikon troparion of Ode 7, portraying the martyrs as an undefeated spiritual army receiving the imperishable crown of eternal life.

[^2022]: Stavrotheotokion of Ode 7, praising the Virgin as the living palace and fiery throne of the incarnate King.

[^2023]: First troparion of Ode 7 (Marian Canon), beseeching the Mother of Life to mortify the passions through tearful repentance.

[^2024]: Second troparion of Ode 7 (Marian Canon), naming the Virgin as unshakeable rampart and guide unto the illumination of compunction.

[^2025]: Third troparion of Ode 7 (Marian Canon), imploring the Mother to beseech her Son for deliverance from demonic malice and Gehenna.

[^2026]: Opening of Troparion 4 of Ode 7 (Marian Canon), continued on physical leaf p235, proclaiming the Virgin's virginitas in partu and post partum.

[^2027]: Conclusion of Troparion 4 of Ode 7 (Marian Canon), continued from physical leaf p234.

[^2028]: Heirmos of Ode 8, contrasting Nebuchadnezzar's lifeless golden idol (Daniel 3:1) with the living, immutable image of God.

[^2029]: First troparion of Ode 8, presenting the crucifixion between two thieves as the suffering of the Justifier on behalf of the unjust (Isaiah 53:12).

[^2030]: Second troparion of Ode 8, meditating upon the bloodied fingers of Christ nailed to the Cross, which abolished the ancient idolatrous blood sacrifices offered to demons (Psalm 105:37-38 [LXX]).

[^2031]: First Martyrikon troparion of Ode 8, celebrating how the martyrs' shed blood dried up the flood of demonic deception.

[^2032]: Second Martyrikon troparion of Ode 8, praising the martyrs whose blood quenched the flames of pagan polytheism.

[^2033]: Stavrotheotokion of Ode 8, depicting the Virgin as the spotless ewe-lamb weeping at the crucifixion of the Unoriginate Lamb.

[^2034]: Heirmos of Ode 8 (Marian Canon), commemorating God's transforming of the furnace flame into cooling dew (Daniel 3:49-50).

[^2035]: First troparion of Ode 8 (Marian Canon), invoking the Virgin's protection amid surrounding tribulations and demonic attacks.

[^2036]: Opening of Troparion 2 of Ode 8 (Marian Canon), continued on physical leaf p236, imploring the awesome Protectress not to ignore the cries of her servants.

[^2037]: Conclusion of Troparion 2 of Ode 8 (Marian Canon), continued from physical leaf p235, celebrating the power of maternal prayer to incline God to mercy.

[^2038]: Third troparion of Ode 8 (Marian Canon), begging the Mother of God to calm internal storms of passion and repel demonic assailants.

[^2039]: Fourth troparion of Ode 8 (Marian Canon), entreating Mary's defense at the dreaded hour of departure from bodily life.

[^2040]: Heirmos of Ode 9, the classic Megalynarion incipit acknowledging that human speech and angelic minds alike fall short in praising the Theotokos.

[^2041]: First troparion of Ode 9, expounding the typology of the binding of Isaac (Genesis 22) and the ram caught in the Sabek thicket (*en phytoi sabek*, LXX Genesis 22:13) as figures of Christ's voluntary sacrifice.

[^2042]: Second troparion of Ode 9, joining Psalm 44:3 [LXX] ("comely in beauty beyond the sons of men") with Isaiah 53:2 ("He hath no form nor comeliness") in the paradox of the Cross.

[^2043]: First Martyrikon troparion of Ode 9, greeting the martyrs as citizens of the heavenly Jerusalem and the assembly of the firstborn (Hebrews 12:22-23).

[^2044]: Second Martyrikon troparion of Ode 9, invoking the martyrs as friends of Christ (John 15:14) to free the soul from carnality.

[^2045]: Stavrotheotokion of Ode 9, narrating the cosmic darkening of the luminaries and the lament of the Virgin accompanied by the Virgin Disciple, Saint John the Theologian (John 19:26-27).

[^2046]: Opening of the Heirmos of Ode 9 (Marian Canon), continued on physical leaf p237, paraphrasing Psalm 117:27 [LXX] ("God is the Lord, and hath appeared unto us").

[^2047]: Conclusion of the Heirmos of Ode 9 (Marian Canon), continued from physical leaf p236.

[^2048]: First troparion of Ode 9 (Marian Canon), appealing to the Virgin's intercession before the Judgment Seat of Christ.

[^2049]: Second troparion of Ode 9 (Marian Canon), asking celestial relief from afflictive passions and condemnation.

[^2050]: Third troparion of Ode 9 (Marian Canon), recalling the deceptive appearance of the forbidden fruit in Eden (Genesis 3:6) which brought death upon humanity.

[^2051]: Fourth troparion of Ode 9 (Marian Canon), praying for the softening and healing of an embittered heart and entry through the gates of repentance.

[^2052]: Rubric concluding Matins: It is truly meet (*Axion Estin*), the Litany, the Exapostilarion, and the customary concluding Lauds/Doxology psalms.

[^2053]: Friday morning Aposticha stichera of Tone 2, dedicated to the Cross and the Martyrs.

[^2054]: First Aposticha sticheron, contrasting the tree of the knowledge of good and evil with the Tree of the Cross which abolished the dominion of death (Hebrews 2:14).

[^2055]: Psalm 89:14, 16 [LXX]. The liturgical incipit with dashes indicates the abbreviation of the full verse text in the printed edition.

[^2056]: Second Aposticha sticheron, expounding 2 Corinthians 8:9 ("though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor").

[^2057]: Psalm 89:17 [LXX].

[^2058]: Martyrikon sticheron at the Aposticha, quoting Wisdom of Solomon 3:1 ("the souls of the righteous are in the hand of God") and Psalm 115:6 [LXX] ("Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of His venerable ones"). Note Slavonic *son* ("sleep/dream") is a recensional variant for *s'mrt'* / *smert'*, reflecting the biblical trope of death as holy sleep.

[^2059]: Theotokion of the Cross (Stavrotheotokion) at the Friday morning Aposticha, set to the canonical prosomoion model "When from the Tree".

[^2060]: Stavrotheotokion expressing the Mother's awe at the mystery of the immortal Word tasting voluntary death.

[^2066]: Third Beatitude troparion, commemorating the martyrs whose physical crushing broke the spiritual power of Satan.

[^2067]: Trinitarian troparion at the Beatitudes, linking the blood of the New Covenant (Hebrews 12:24) with Trinitarian illumination.

[^2068]: Concluding Stavrotheotokion of the Beatitudes.

[^2071]: First sticheron at "Lord, I have cried" on Friday evening, chanted twice, celebrating the martyrs' victory over idol worship and standing before the throne of God.

[^2072]: Second sticheron at "Lord, I have cried," honoring the Holy Hierarchs and Venerable Doctors who formulated Orthodox dogma and expelled heresy from the Church.

[^2073]: Idiomelon/Martyrikon stichera at "Lord, I have cried" in Tone 2.

[^2074]: First Martyrikon sticheron, contrasting transient earthly pleasure with celestial bliss.

[^2075]: Second Martyrikon sticheron, exalting the intercession of the martyrs in overthrowing demonic deception.

[^2076]: Third Martyrikon sticheron, dramatizing the bold confession of the martyrs before pagan judges.

[^2077]: Tone 2 Friday evening Dogmatikon Theotokion, masterfully setting forth Old Testament typological antitypes: the shadow of the law yielding to grace (Hebrews 10:1), the unburnt bush foreshadowing virginity in childbearing (Exodus 3:2), the pillar of fire yielding to the Sun of Righteousness (Malachi 4:2), and Moses yielding to Christ (John 1:17).

[^2078]: Vespers rubrics: the ancient hymn Phos Hilaron (*O Joyful Light*), the Friday evening Prokeimenon (Psalm 58:10, 18 [LXX]), and the evening prayer *Kataxioson* (*Vouchsafe, O Lord*).

[^2080]: First Aposticha sticheron, venerating the healing and exorcistic power of the relics of the holy martyrs.

[^2081]: Psalm 64:5 [LXX], the canonical verse for the commemoration of the departed.

[^2082]: Hymn for the Departed (Поко́инъ) sticheron for the departed, contrasting earthly vanity (Job 14:2; Psalm 102:15 [LXX]) with the universal resurrection at the last trumpet (1 Corinthians 15:52; 1 Thessalonians 4:16-17).

[^2083]: Psalm 24:13 [LXX].

[^2084]: Opening of the famous Idiomelon for the departed (attributed to St. John of Damascus), continued on physical leaf p240, reflecting on the terror of the soul at the moment of death.

[^2086]: Concluding Theotokion at the Aposticha of Friday Vespers.

[^3507]: Saturday Matins, Kathisma 1 Sessional Hymn 1 (Martyricon), Tone 3: *Благодꙋ́шное терпѣ́нїа ва́шегѡ, побѣдѝ кѡ́зни ѕлонача́лнагѡ врага̀...*

[^3509]: Saturday Matins, Kathisma 1 Sessional Hymn 2 (Martyricon): *Сїѧ́ете вѣ́рою пресвѣ́тлаа свѣти̑ла Ст҃і́и, недꙋ́гꙋющихъ вра́чеве...*

[^3510]: Saturday Matins, Kathisma 1 Theotokion: *Тѧ̀ хода́тайствовавшꙋю спасенїе ро́да на́шегѡ, воспѣва́емъ Бцⷣе Дѣ́во...*
